title: Divorce (Gittin 90b)
hook: divorce needs a written document; the Talmud says the altar weeps, yet it is permitted

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ketubah, the marriage contract the wife keeps. Your line: protection in writing. Today, a harder page.

Some readers say the last page of a tractate is where the rabbis leave something they want remembered. Tractate Gittin, the book of divorce, spends page after page on details: who writes the document, who signs it, how it's delivered. Then, on its final page, the Mishnah records an argument about when a man may divorce his wife, and the Talmud adds one sentence. Divorce is permitted. And yet when a man divorces the wife of his youth, even the altar sheds tears.
screen: `PAGE AFTER PAGE OF DETAILS.` → `THE LAST PAGE.` → `EVEN THE ALTAR SHEDS TEARS.`

segments.voice: Get. A get is the Jewish document of divorce. First, it has to be written. The Torah describes a man who, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "writeth her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand." Not a word spoken in anger, not a door slammed: a written document, carefully made, delivered into her hand. The care slows things down, and it gives her proof that she is free. Second, the argument. The Mishnah records three views about the grounds. The school of Shammai says only for a serious sexual wrong. The school of Hillel says even if she spoiled his cooking. Rabbi Akiva says even if he found someone more beautiful. The rabbis argue, out loud, about how easy it should be to end a marriage, and the law, as later codes follow it, does permit divorce. Third, the tears. Right after this argument, the Talmud quotes a sage: whoever divorces his first wife, even the altar sheds tears over him. It draws on the prophet Malachi, who rebukes men who cover the altar with weeping, and calls the abandoned wife "the wife of thy covenant." The law stays the law. A marriage that cannot go on may end. But the text refuses to pretend an ending is nothing. Permission and grief, side by side on the same page, like so much of this week: rest given a definition, joy given a frame, a wife given a contract, and now a document that frees, written next to tears.
screen: `WRITTEN, AND GIVEN IN HER HAND.` · `SHAMMAI, HILLEL, AKIVA.` · `EVEN THE ALTAR SHEDS TEARS.` · `PERMISSION AND GRIEF, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `EVEN THE ALTAR WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that ended: a marriage, a friendship, a job, a home, a version of yourself. You don't have to decide whether it was right; just let both be true for a minute, that it was allowed to end and that it's all right to grieve it. If an ending feels too heavy to carry alone, you can call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Get. The Jewish document of divorce, written with care and given into the wife's hand, permitted, and grieved. Today's word.
Your line: even the altar weeps. An ending can be allowed and still be mourned. Go gently until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Orthodox and Conservative communities a get is written by a scribe and given before a rabbinical court, alongside any civil divorce; Reform Judaism generally accepts a civil divorce, and some Reform rabbis offer a ritual of parting.

chat.says: Does Jewish law allow divorce, or does it forbid it?
options: It allows divorce by a careful written document, yet the Talmud says even the altar weeps.
It forbids divorce; the Talmud says a marriage can never be undone once made.
It allows divorce freely, and the rabbis never argued over whether it was sad.
